analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan borrowers wipe out their debt in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current bankruptcy law, student loans are the rare debt you almost never escape—you must prove 'undue hardship' in a separate lawsuit just to try. This bill would delete that rule, so student loans would be treated like credit card debt, medical bills, and every other consumer debt: dischargeable when someone's finances collapse. It was referred to the Judiciary Committee, which took no action, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers who are in genuine financial distress and would file for bankruptcy. Today, §523(a)(8) of the bankruptcy code excludes student loans from discharge unless the borrower files a separate 'adversary proceeding' and proves repaying them would cause undue hardship—a standard many courts apply so strictly that most borrowers cannot meet it. Striking that exception would let them treat their student loans like any other unsecured debt in a bankruptcy case, applying to cases filed after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Distressed student loan borrowers in bankruptcy

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the bankruptcy code's student loan discharge exception by striking §523(a)(8), so student loans become dischargeable like other consumer debts in cases filed after enactment.
Makes a conforming change to the Chapter 13 plan-confirmation rules (§1328(a)(2)) so student loans are treated consistently across bankruptcy chapters.

Removes the requirement that borrowers file a separate lawsuit against their lender and prove 'undue hardship'—the barrier that makes relief from student debt in bankruptcy extremely rare in practice.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and the federal government, which now holds most student loans, would absorb losses when borrowers discharge loans they could otherwise collect for decades; loan losses would ultimately fall on taxpayers, and lenders might price that risk into future student loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal government and student lenders

drawbacks.text: Lenders and the federal government lose the money owed by borrowers who discharge their loans, and those losses would ultimately be borne by taxpayers or priced into higher interest rates on future student loans.

Critics of removing the undue-hardship rule argue it would encourage some borrowers to file bankruptcy soon after graduating—when their incomes are lowest—rather than pay off loans they could eventually afford, raising borrowing costs for everyone else.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers in genuine long-term distress, the benefit is real: today's rule is so restrictive that most get no relief even after proving years of hardship. The cost is that the government—the country's dominant student lender—would take larger losses in bankruptcy, which could mean more pressure on taxpayers or somewhat higher loan pricing. That tradeoff is debatable, which is a fair argument for Congress to have; the bill never received one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee on October 4, 2024, and the committee took no action before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the Student Borrower Bankruptcy Relief Act of 2024 on October 4, 2024, joined by 19 Democratic cosponsors.

The bill would amend the bankruptcy code by striking the §523(a)(8) exception, making student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy, with a conforming change to §1328(a)(2), applying to cases filed after enactment.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction; that was the bill's final action of record.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders and the federal government keep their current position: student loans remain collectible for decades and are almost never dischargeable in bankruptcy. Borrowers in distress got no relief, and Congress never debated the change.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy.

for.name: 19 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action—no hearing, markup, or vote—so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past committee referral.

industries.industry: Student loan holders and the federal government as lender
industries.note: Student loans would become collectible like ordinary consumer debt instead of surviving bankruptcy for decades. Because the federal government now holds most student loans, discharges would translate into federal losses.
Accounts that can be wiped out in bankruptcy are less valuable to service and collect than loans that survive nearly every bankruptcy filing, reducing the long stream of servicing revenue.
Other unsecured creditors in a borrower's bankruptcy would sometimes receive a larger share once student loans stop holding a protected priority, though this effect is secondary.
